The API exposes `GET /health`, which returns a JSON readiness result, and a random-challenge flow:

- `POST /v1/challenges` issues a one-time random challenge (nonce) bound to a tenant and workload, with a bounded TTL. The JSON body must include non-empty `tenant_id` and `workload_id` and an optional integer `ttl_seconds` (default 300, bounded 30..900); a missing, blank, wrong-typed or out-of-range field is `422` and writes no state. On success it returns `201` with `challenge_id`, the one-time `nonce`, a UTC RFC3339 `issued_at` and `expires_at`, and status `pending`; only the nonce's SHA-256 digest is persisted, never the nonce itself, and challenges survive restarts. Issuance has its own persistent per-tenant/workload rate limit described below (five per UTC natural minute), entirely separate from the one-time-grant budget: after all fields validate, the sixth legal request in a UTC minute stably receives `429` (serial or concurrent — exactly five requests in the minute get a `201` and a consumable pending challenge), a rejected request creates no challenge and never mints, returns or persists a nonce, and a counter read/write failure is `500 detail "rate limit unavailable"` with neither a half challenge nor a half count left behind.
- `POST /v1/challenges/{challenge_id}/consume` consumes a pending, unexpired challenge by presenting its nonce to prove freshness.
- `GET /v1/challenges/{challenge_id}` is the read-only challenge status query. The path identifier must be a canonical lowercase UUID and both required query parameters `tenant_id` and `workload_id` must be present and non-blank; a missing/blank/repeated scope parameter, an unknown parameter, a malformed identifier or a non-empty request body is `422` with detail `invalid challenge query` before storage is touched. A challenge that does not exist or does not belong to both scope parameters returns one indistinguishable `404` with detail `challenge not found`. On success it returns `200` with exactly `challenge_id`, `issued_at`, `expires_at`, `status`, `changed_at`, `evidence_id`, `evidence_format`, `verification_result`, all timestamps UTC RFC3339: a consumed-less challenge reads as `pending` while the query instant is before `expires_at` and `expired` at or after it (expiry is derived at read time and never written back), a consumed challenge with no evidence is `consumed`, associated evidence still `received` is `evidence_received`, and the first verification settles the phase to `verified` (`verification_result` `accepted`) or `rejected` (`rejected`); `changed_at` is the timestamp that decided the phase — `consumed_at`, the evidence's `verified_at`/`received_at`, `expires_at` or `issued_at`. With no evidence, `evidence_id` and `evidence_format` are `null`; `verification_result` is `null` until the evidence settles. The query issues only SELECTs: it performs no expiry writeback, appends no event, audit or idempotency record, consumes no challenge-issuance, verification-admission or one-time-grant release budget, and never returns the nonce, nonce digest, evidence text or digest, plugin text or private key material. A concurrent consume/receipt/verify that commits first is the phase a query observes; against the same committed state repeated queries are byte-stable. A storage read failure is a sanitized `500` with detail `challenge status unavailable`.
- `POST /v1/evidence` receives attestation evidence for a pending, unexpired challenge. The JSON body must include `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `challenge_id`, `nonce` (unpadded base64url), `evidence_format`, and `evidence`. On success it returns `201` with `evidence_id`, `challenge_id`, status `received`, and a UTC RFC3339 `received_at`, and consumes the challenge in the same transaction so it cannot be reused. Only the SHA-256 digest of the evidence is persisted — never the evidence itself. Errors: `404` unknown/mismatched challenge, `401` wrong nonce, `409` already consumed or received, `410` expired, `422` invalid fields.
- `POST /v1/evidence/{evidence_id}/verify` verifies previously received evidence. The JSON body must include non-empty `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `nonce` (unpadded base64url) and `evidence` (non-empty string). Only evidence belonging to the same tenant and workload, together with its challenge, is processed: the nonce is checked against the challenge and the evidence is checked to be byte-identical to what was received (SHA-256 digest comparison). The first verification settles the record atomically (`verified` or `rejected`); later calls return the stored conclusion and never re-run the verifier. Both outcomes return `200` with `evidence_id`, `challenge_id`, `status` and a UTC RFC3339 `verified_at`. Errors: `404` unknown/mismatched evidence, `401` wrong nonce, `422` invalid fields/format or evidence digest mismatch (including an `evidence_format` with no registered verifier), `500` verifier plugin failure or, for X.509 evidence, an unavailable revocation registry (no partial state is left behind; the evidence stays `received` and can be re-verified after recovery). Verification has its own persistent per-tenant/workload admission budget of five verifier entries per UTC natural minute, entirely separate from the challenge-issuance and one-time-grant budgets: only a request whose evidence is still `received` and whose identity, challenge binding, nonce, digest and format checks all passed atomically reserves a slot (so every earlier error above and every idempotent replay of a settled evidence spends nothing); the sixth such request in a minute receives `429` with detail `verification rate limit exceeded` and a whole-seconds `Retry-After` header to the next UTC minute, writing nothing (no counter, settlement, lifecycle event or audit row). A reserved slot is durable across restarts and is never refunded — a verifier plugin failure or an unavailable revocation registry keeps it while the evidence stays `received` — and a counter read/write failure is `500` with detail `verification rate limit unavailable`, again leaving the evidence `received` for a later retry. As with receipt, the raw evidence is never persisted, logged, or returned — only its digest, the settlement status, timestamp, and a fixed service-defined result code (`accepted`/`rejected`) derived solely from the verifier's verdict are stored.
- `POST /v1/trust-roots` configures an attestation trust root for a tenant and workload. The JSON body must include non-empty `tenant_id`, `workload_id` and `root_pem`, plus an optional non-empty `name`. `root_pem` must be a parseable X.509 CA certificate; anything else (including any private-key material) is rejected and never stored. On success it returns `201` with `root_id`, `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `name` and a UTC RFC3339 `created_at`. Trust roots are persisted and survive restarts. Errors: `409` the same certificate is already configured for this tenant and workload, `422` invalid fields, unparseable PEM, or a non-CA certificate.
- `POST /v1/trust-roots/{root_id}/retire` retires a configured trust root — a terminal `active` -> `retired` transition that happens exactly once. The path `root_id` must be a canonical lowercase UUID (a missing, blank, whitespace-padded or non-canonical value is `422` and never reads or modifies the root); the body carries exactly two non-empty strings, `tenant_id` and `workload_id` — a missing, blank, wrong-typed, incomplete or unknown field is `422` and writes no state. An unknown root or one whose ownership disagrees with either body field is an indistinguishable `404` (existence is never revealed). On the first legal request the row is atomically set to `retired` with its first-and-final UTC RFC3339 `retired_at`, under the same trust-root row lock X.509 verification takes; success returns `200` with compact JSON containing exactly `root_id`, `status` (fixed `retired`) and `retired_at` in that key order, all JSON strings, terminated by a single newline (no floats or non-finite values, no extra metadata). A repeat retire returns `409`, rewrites neither `retired_at` nor any other state and appends no audit or other record; concurrent retires of one root settle as exactly one `200` plus stable `409`s. A write or commit failure returns `500` after a full rollback, leaving the original status and time intact (and the same request succeeds after recovery). Retirement survives restarts. Retiring a root does not erase or alter anything else — HMAC format handling, custom plugins and existing revocation registrations are unchanged — and the same certificate still cannot be re-created under the same tenant and workload (still `409`), so retirement cannot be bypassed.
- `GET /v1/trust-roots` is the read-only trust-root lifecycle query: it lists configured roots for one tenant/workload in stable `(created_at, root_id)` ascending order with keyset pagination; the request body is always empty (any non-empty body, including whitespace, is a `422` before any state is read). `tenant_id` and `workload_id` are required non-empty query parameters. Results may be narrowed by `root_id` (a canonical lowercase UUID), `name` (an exact, non-blank text value), `status` (exactly `active` or `retired`), and by an inclusive creation window `created_after`/`created_before`, both explicit UTC RFC3339 timestamps (`Z` or `+00:00`; a naive or non-UTC offset is rejected); `created_after` must not be later than `created_before`. An extra, repeated, missing/blank/whitespace, wrong-typed or malformed parameter (including an illegal identifier, status or timestamp, or an inverted window) returns `422` and reads no state. An explicit `root_id` that is unknown or belongs to another tenant/workload is one indistinguishable `404`; a `name` or other range filter that matches nothing is simply an empty range, never an error. Pagination is cursor-driven: omitting `cursor` or sending an explicit empty string starts before the smallest registration and fixes a replayable snapshot; the exclusive cursor boundary is the last returned `(created_at, root_id)` position, and results stay in stable ascending order by creation time and immutable root id. Cursors are opaque, HMAC-authenticated tokens carrying a distinct trust-root cursor kind tag, bound to the scope, every active filter *and* the fixed replayable snapshot — a forged, tampered, cross-scope, cross-filter, cross-snapshot or foreign-family (rewrap batch, release-grant audit, compliance audit, proof-lifecycle, decisions, revocations or rewrap job) cursor returns `422` and reads no state. The snapshot is fixed to a *business commit boundary*: creation and the terminal retirement share one per-scope, gap-free, strictly increasing sequence (a dedicated counter row read under lock — `FOR UPDATE` on locking backends, the existing `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` serialization on SQLite), and each root records the sequence of its own retirement; replaying any of the snapshot's cursors always returns the identical page in the identical order — never duplicating or skipping an entry, and presenting exactly the status and retirement time the range had at first-query time even while roots are concurrently retired or new roots registered. Databases written before the sequence existed are upgraded on open on every backend (the nullable columns are added when missing, legacy creations are numbered per scope in stable `(created_at, root_id)` order and legacy retirements immediately after them, the per-scope counter is seeded at that maximum, and the unique `(scope, commit_seq)` plus scoped keyset indexes are built). Registrations or retirements committed after the first query appear only in a new cursor-less first query. The compact JSON response, terminated by a single newline, has keys in exactly the order `trust_roots`, `next_cursor` (empty at the end), `complete`; each entry carries the creation-response fields `root_id`, `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `name` and `created_at` (in that order), then the current-as-of-snapshot `status` and a UTC RFC3339 or `null` `retired_at` (null for every root not yet retired by the snapshot). All text and timestamps are JSON strings and no floats, `-0.0` or non-finite values ever appear; certificate PEM, private keys, evidence and exception text are never returned, stored in a new field, or logged. The handler issues only reads of committed state, never writes or retires a root, appends no audit, and returns no half page: a storage/service failure is a `500` with the half page discarded entirely. Trust-root creation and retirement, X.509 verification, certificate revocation and the existing policy and authorization entry points behave exactly as before; scope isolation, cross-restart retention and the never-revive-after-retirement semantics are unchanged.
- `POST /v1/revocations` registers a trust-root-scoped X.509 certificate revocation. The JSON body must include non-empty `tenant_id` and `workload_id`, a canonical lowercase-UUID `trust_root_id` that belongs to exactly that tenant and workload (an unknown or cross-scope root is an indistinguishable `404`), `certificate_fingerprint` as the unpadded base64url SHA-256 of the certificate's DER encoding (exactly 32 raw bytes, no padding), and `effective_at` as a UTC RFC3339 timestamp (`Z` or `+00:00`; a naive or non-UTC offset is rejected). A missing, blank, wrong-typed or malformed field returns `422` and writes no state. A past effective time is in effect immediately; a future one takes effect once that instant arrives. On success it returns `201` with compact JSON containing exactly `revocation_id`, `trust_root_id`, `certificate_fingerprint` and `effective_at`; registrations are persisted, survive restarts, and never store certificate material or secrets. Within one trust root the same fingerprint is registered at most once — a repeat (including one with a different effective time) returns `409` and never merges or overwrites the first registration — while distinct fingerprints under the same root are independent rows; concurrent duplicate registrations settle with exactly one `201`, every loser receiving a stable `409` and no duplicate row. The scope, trust root, fingerprint and effective time are a single atomic write: any failure during the locked lookups or the insert/commit returns `500` after a full rollback, leaving no half record (and the same registration succeeds once storage recovers). Revocations are isolated per tenant and workload and are scoped to a single trust root — a registration under one root never affects evidence anchored to another root even for an identical certificate.
- `GET /v1/revocations` is the read-only revocation registry query: it lists registered revocations for one tenant/workload/trust root in stable `(effective_at, revocation_id)` ascending order with keyset pagination; the request body is always empty (any non-empty body, including whitespace, is a `422` before any state is read) and no other query parameters are accepted. `tenant_id`, `workload_id` and `trust_root_id` (a canonical UUID) are required non-empty query parameters. Results may be narrowed by `revocation_id` (a canonical UUID), `certificate_fingerprint` (canonical unpadded base64url of exactly 32 bytes), and by an inclusive effective window `effective_after`/`effective_before`, both explicit UTC RFC3339 timestamps (`Z` or `+00:00`; a naive or non-UTC offset is rejected); `effective_after` must not be later than `effective_before`. A missing/blank/whitespace/typed-wrong parameter, an unknown parameter, an illegal identifier, fingerprint or timestamp, or an inverted window returns `422` and writes no state. An explicit `trust_root_id`, `revocation_id` or `certificate_fingerprint` that is unknown, belongs to another tenant/workload, or (for the fingerprint and revocation id) to another trust root returns one indistinguishable `404` without revealing which; a query with no explicit resource whose filters match nothing is simply an empty range. Pagination is cursor-driven: omitting `cursor` or sending an explicit empty string starts before the smallest registration, and the exclusive cursor boundary is the last returned `(effective_at, revocation_id)` position. Cursors are opaque, HMAC-authenticated tokens carrying a distinct revocation cursor kind tag, bound to the scope, every active filter *and* the fixed replayable snapshot — a forged, tampered, cross-scope, cross-filter or foreign-family (rewrap batch, release-grant audit, compliance audit) cursor returns `422` and reads no state. The first (cursor-less) query of a range fixes a replayable snapshot: replaying any of its cursors always returns the identical page in the identical order, never duplicating or skipping an entry and unaffected by registrations committed concurrently or afterwards; registrations committed after that first query appear only in a new cursor-less first query. The compact JSON response, terminated by a single newline, has keys in exactly the order `revocations`, `next_cursor` (empty at the end), `complete`; each entry contains only the four JSON-string fields `revocation_id`, `trust_root_id`, `certificate_fingerprint` and `effective_at` (in the registration response order) — no floats, `-0.0` or non-finite values ever appear, and the query neither computes nor rewrites a certificate's current status: future-effective registrations are listed with their recorded time. The handler issues only reads of committed state, never writes, settles, creates an audit row or modifies a registration, and returns no half page: a registry/storage failure is a `500` with no partial result. Registration creation, concurrent uniqueness, future effectiveness and the X.509 real-time rejection behavior are unchanged.
- `POST /v1/crls` registers an X.509 v2 CRL as a trust-root-scoped revocation source. The JSON body must include exactly non-empty `tenant_id` and `workload_id`, a canonical lowercase-UUID `trust_root_id`, and a PEM `crl_pem`; any other field is rejected. Error order is fixed: a missing, blank, wrong-typed or non-UUID field, or any intrinsic CRL defect — non-PEM/invalid ASN.1, a body that is not an X.509 v2 CRL (the v2-only `CRLNumber` extension is required), a missing `nextUpdate`, a `thisUpdate` after the receipt instant, a `nextUpdate` not strictly later than both `thisUpdate` and the receipt instant, or an illegal or duplicated revoked-certificate serial — is a `422` produced before storage is touched (and therefore never reveals whether the trust root exists). The named trust root is then read in the request's exact tenant/workload scope: an unknown or cross-scope root is an indistinguishable `404`. The issuer distinguished name must equal the trust-root subject and the CRL signature must verify under the trust-root public key; either mismatch is a `422` (only after the root is found). Within one trust root, an identical `CRLNumber`, a byte-identical CRL body, or any number not strictly higher than the current maximum `CRLNumber` returns `409`; only a strictly higher number becomes the current snapshot, and older snapshots are retained immutably. Concurrent equal-number/equal-content registrations settle with exactly one `201`, every loser receiving a stable `409`. On success the snapshot and all of its revoked entries commit as one atomic write and the response is `201` with compact JSON containing exactly `crl_id`, `trust_root_id`, `crl_number`, `this_update`, `next_update` and `revoked_count`; `revoked_count` counts only entries whose `revocationDate` has already arrived at receipt time. The CRL body, certificate material and exception details are never returned, logged or persisted (only parsed metadata, a SHA-256 of the CRL DER and the revoked issuer-DN/serial/date triples are stored). A storage or service failure during the locked lookups or the multi-row insert/commit returns `500` after a full rollback: no partial snapshot or entry survives and the previous snapshot stays current. CRLs are isolated per tenant/workload/trust root.
- `POST /v1/workload-identities` registers a workload identity profile that constrains which X.509 leaf certificate an anchored chain may present. The JSON body must include non-empty `tenant_id` and `workload_id`, a canonical lowercase-UUID `trust_root_id` that belongs to exactly that tenant and workload (an unknown or cross-scope root is an indistinguishable `404`), and a non-empty `claims` list. Each claim is an object with three required non-empty strings, `issuer`, `subject` and `uri`, holding the *parsed* comparison values of a leaf certificate: the issuer distinguished name and subject distinguished name rendered as RFC4514 strings (e.g. `CN=test-intermediate`), and one subjectAlternativeName URI (e.g. `spiffe://example.org/workload/payments`); a missing, blank, wrong-typed or malformed field, a non-canonical UUID, an empty `claims` list, a claim missing/blank on any of the three fields, or any unknown extra field returns `422` and writes no state. On success it returns `201` with compact JSON containing exactly `profile_id`, `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `trust_root_id`, `claims` (the de-duplicated claims in first-seen order) and a UTC RFC3339 `created_at`; profiles are persisted, survive restarts, and store only the non-sensitive comparison strings — never certificate material, evidence, private keys or secrets. Claims compare as an unordered set: within one trust root, registering the identical claim set (regardless of entry order or duplicate entries) returns `409` and never overwrites the first profile, while a different claim set is saved as an independent profile. The profile and all its claims are one atomic write taken under the trust-root row lock; a failure during the locked lookups or the insert/commit returns `500` after a full rollback, leaving no half profile. Concurrent registrations of the same claim set under the same trust root settle with exactly one `201` and stable `409`s for every loser (a unique `(trust_root_id, claim-set fingerprint)` constraint backs this), and distinct sets never conflict.
- `GET /v1/workload-identities` queries registered profiles. The request body is always empty (any non-empty body, including whitespace, is a `422` before any state is read) and the range is fixed entirely by query parameters: required non-empty `tenant_id`, `workload_id` and `trust_root_id` (a canonical UUID), plus an optional canonical `profile_id`. A missing, blank, wrong-typed or malformed parameter (including an unknown query parameter) returns `422`; an explicitly named `profile_id` that is unknown or outside the tenant/workload/trust-root range returns `404`; an unknown trust root with no profile filter is simply an empty range. On success it returns `200` with compact JSON (single trailing newline) containing an array of profiles sorted by `created_at` then `profile_id`; an empty range is `[]`. Each element carries the registration fields (`profile_id`, `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `trust_root_id`, `claims`, `created_at`) plus the lifecycle `status` (`active` or `revoked`); revoked profiles remain listed here. The handler issues only reads of committed state, and a registry failure is a `500` with no partial result.
- `PUT /v1/workload-identities/{profile_id}` replaces a profile's complete claim set. The path identifier must be a canonical lowercase UUID with no surrounding whitespace (a missing, blank or malformed identifier, including an empty path segment, is `422`). The JSON body carries the same fields as registration — non-empty `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, canonical `trust_root_id`, and a non-empty `claims` list with the same per-claim rules — and a missing, blank, wrong-typed, empty, malformed or unknown field returns `422` and writes nothing. The profile must exist in exactly the body's scope and trust root (unknown/cross-scope is `404`); an already-revoked profile is terminal and a replacement attempt returns `409` and moves nothing, even when the submitted set equals its last committed set. The replacement is whole-set: the old claims are deleted and the new ones inserted in one atomic transaction with the profile row, so `profile_id`, ownership/scope and `created_at` never change, while `updated_at` is set; a write or commit failure returns `500` after a full rollback and the old claims, status and timestamps are all unchanged. Resubmitting the profile's own current claim set (any order, duplicates collapsed) is an idempotent no-op returning `200` with the current result and never minting or rewriting `updated_at`; requesting a set already owned by a *different* profile under the same trust root returns `409` and moves nothing; concurrent updates based on the same original set settle with exactly one effective write — a request whose requested set just won is answered `200` with that current result, any other stale write receives `409`, and a revocation racing the replacement leaves the revoked profile's last set intact. Success returns `200` with compact JSON containing the original profile fields (`profile_id`, scope, `trust_root_id`, `claims`, `created_at`) plus a UTC RFC3339 `updated_at`.
- `DELETE /v1/workload-identities/{profile_id}` revokes a profile. The path identifier must be a canonical lowercase UUID with no surrounding whitespace (an empty or malformed segment is `422`) and the JSON body carries exactly `tenant_id`, `workload_id` and `trust_root_id`; a missing, blank, wrong-typed, malformed or unknown field returns `422` without writing state. An unknown profile or one outside the body's scope/trust root returns `404`. The active → `revoked` transition is a single guarded atomic update under the trust-root lock; repeating the revocation returns `409` and never rewrites the stored `revoked_at`, and a write/commit failure returns `500` after a full rollback, leaving the profile, status and revocation time unchanged. Success returns `200` with compact JSON containing the original profile fields plus `"revoked": true` and a UTC RFC3339 `revoked_at` (and the existing `updated_at` when the profile had been replaced). A revoked profile stays queryable with status `revoked` but no longer participates in X.509 identity gating; its last committed claims are retained.
- `POST /v1/policies` creates a versioned release policy scoped to a tenant and workload. The JSON body must include non-empty `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `name` and `rule`. A rule is exactly one of `{"claim": "<top-level claim name>", "equals": <scalar>}` (scalar = string, number, boolean or null), `{"path": ["<segment>", ...], "equals": <scalar>}`, `{"all": [rule, ...]}`, `{"any": [rule, ...]}` (both non-empty lists) or `{"not": rule}`; any other shape is rejected with `422`. A `path` leaf names an object field path *inside* the top-level claims: it must carry at least one segment, at most eight segments in total, and every segment must be either a non-empty, non-whitespace string of at most 128 characters, or the exact wildcard object `{"wildcard": true}` — a segment carrying exactly one `wildcard` key whose value is the JSON boolean `true` (no other key may appear, and `1`, `false`, a string or any other value is invalid); a missing or empty `path`, a blank, over-long or wrong-typed segment, an object segment of any other form (empty object, an extra key, or a non-`true` value), more than eight segments, a missing comparison, a comparison that is an object or array where a scalar is required, an unknown sibling key (on any node), or an illegally nested rule is `422` — no version is allocated and no state is written. The literal string `"*"` stays an ordinary field name. Each string segment names exactly one JSON object field and segments are read strictly top to bottom starting at the top-level `claims` (e.g. `["tenant", "region"]` reads `claims.tenant.region`); a dot embedded in a segment is a literal character of that one field name and never splits it. A `{"wildcard": true}` segment expands only when the value at that position is a JSON array, producing one candidate per element; several wildcard segments expand left to right into the full set of candidate paths, and the string segments around them still match same-named object fields only. An empty array, a non-array at a wildcard position, a missing intermediate field, or a scalar/array/non-object met while another segment still has to descend yields no candidates for that branch. The terminal values of all complete candidates then use the same type-strict scalar comparison as `claim` rules, with any-candidate semantics: a leaf is true when at least one candidate satisfies `equals`, `in`, `contains` or an `lt`/`lte`/`gt`/`gte` ordering (a complete candidate may itself be a scalar, null, array or object), and `exists` is true when at least one complete candidate is readable; zero candidates make the leaf false. A terminal array candidate keeps the ordinary `contains` rule (the candidate must itself be an array holding an equal element). Path and claim leaves may be nested together inside `all`, `any` and `not`; evaluation keeps short-circuit semantics. Wildcards are path segments, not rule nodes, so they consume none of the 256-node/32-depth budgets. Creating a policy with an existing `(tenant_id, workload_id, name)` allocates the next integer `version` (the first is `1`) and retains every older version unchanged; scope or name isolation restarts the sequence at `1`. Concurrent creators never share or skip a version. On success it returns `201` with `policy_id`, the scope, `name`, `version`, the submitted `rule`, and a UTC RFC3339 `created_at`. Policies are persisted and survive restarts; only the rule tree (claim names, path segments and expected scalars — never evidence or claim values) is stored. The creation additionally accepts an optional `Idempotency-Key` request header whose value is 1 to 64 visible ASCII characters (`0x21`–`0x7E`, never empty, whitespace-padded or containing control or non-ASCII characters) and which may appear exactly once; the JSON body contract is unchanged. When the header is absent the original one-new-version-per-valid-request semantics apply exactly and old callers need no adjustment. A duplicated header or an illegal key value is an indistinguishable `422` with detail `invalid idempotency key`, raised after the body (including rule) validation but before any state is read or written, so it creates no policy, allocates no version number or lifecycle commit sequence and persists no record. Within one `(tenant_id, workload_id)` scope the first legal keyed creation atomically writes the new policy row, its lifecycle commit sequence and a persistent idempotency record in a single transaction; the same key in another tenant or workload is an independent entry and never conflicts. Every later same-key request whose equivalence range — the same `name` and a rule tree that normalizes to the same canonical JSON under the existing rule normalization (key order and whitespace are insignificant) — matches returns that first `201` byte-for-byte, preserving the original `policy_id`, `version` and `created_at`: it creates no version, recomputes no version number or commit sequence and changes no existing policy. Reusing a key in the same scope with a different `name` or a different normalized rule tree is a stable `409` with detail `idempotency key reused with a different request` that leaves the original policy and record untouched. Concurrent same-key requests with identical content settle as exactly one policy version whose identical first response every request receives, while different requests competing for one key are ordered by the unique `(scope, key)` constraint so at most one succeeds and the rest stably receive that `409`. An invalid rule, or any write or commit failure, fully rolls back: no half policy or half record remains, no version or commit sequence is consumed, and the key stays free for the same legal request to retry; any persistence failure is reported as `500` with detail `policy write failed`. The record is created additively when a database written before it existed is first opened, survives restarts, and stores — apart from its own id and creation time — only the scope, the key, a SHA-256 fingerprint of the canonical scope/name/normalized-rule identity and the exact first `201` response body; no evidence, claims material, capabilities, keys or exception text is stored, and the record is never part of the public policy listing or query.
- `POST /v1/policies/{policy_id}/retire` retires one concrete policy version — a terminal `active` -> `retired` transition that happens exactly once. The retirement record, response and logs contain no rule tree, evidence, claims, nonce, capability, payload, key material or exception text.

Pagination is cursor-driven: omitting `cursor` or sending an explicit empty string starts before the smallest policy version and fixes a replayable snapshot; the exclusive cursor boundary is the last returned `(created_at, policy_id)` position, and results stay in stable ascending order by creation time and immutable policy id. Cursors are opaque, HMAC-authenticated tokens carrying a distinct policy cursor kind tag, bound to the scope, every active filter *and* the fixed replayable snapshot — a forged, tampered, cross-scope, cross-filter, cross-snapshot or foreign-family (rewrap batch, release-grant audit, compliance audit, proof-lifecycle, decisions, revocations, trust roots or rewrap job) cursor returns `422` and reads no state. The snapshot is fixed to a *business commit boundary*: version creation and the terminal retirement share one per-scope, gap-free, strictly increasing sequence (a dedicated counter row read under lock — `FOR UPDATE` on locking backends, the existing `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` serialization on SQLite), and each version records the sequence of its own retirement; replaying any of the snapshot's cursors always returns the identical page in the identical order — never duplicating or skipping an entry, and presenting exactly the status and retirement time the range had at first-query time even while versions are concurrently retired or new versions created. Databases written before the sequence existed are upgraded on open on every backend (the nullable columns are added when missing, legacy creations are numbered per scope in stable `(created_at, policy_id)` order and legacy retirements immediately after them, the per-scope counter is seeded at that maximum, and the unique `(scope, commit_seq)` plus scoped keyset indexes are built). Versions created or retirements committed after the first query appear only in a new cursor-less first query. The compact JSON response, terminated by a single newline, has keys in exactly the order `policies`, `next_cursor` (empty at the end), `complete`; each entry carries the creation-response fields `policy_id`, `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `name`, `version`, `rule` and `created_at` (in that order), then the current-as-of-snapshot `status` and a UTC RFC3339 or `null` `retired_at` (null for every version not yet retired by the snapshot). The rule is returned exactly as created: its `number` values round-trip verbatim, including decimals and `-0.0`, while every other field is a JSON string, integer (`version`), boolean or null — no other float or non-finite value ever appears. Evidence, claim values, capabilities, keys and exception text are never returned, stored in a new field, or logged. The handler issues only reads of committed state, never writes or retires a version, appends no audit, and returns no half page: a storage/service failure is a `500` with the half page discarded entirely. Policy creation, retirement, decision evaluation and the existing decision, trust-root and authorization entry points behave exactly as before; scope isolation, versioning, cross-restart retention and the never-revive-after-retirement semantics are unchanged.

- `POST /v1/evidence/{evidence_id}/decisions` evaluates a verified piece of evidence against one policy version and records an auditable release decision. The JSON body must include non-empty `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `nonce` (unpadded base64url), `evidence` (the same bytes received/verified — checked by SHA-256 digest, never re-verified and never persisted) and `policy_id`. Both the evidence and the policy must belong to exactly the request's tenant and workload (`404` if either is unknown or cross-scope), the evidence must already be settled `verified` (`409` for received or rejected evidence), and the policy version must not have been retired via `POST /v1/policies/{policy_id}/retire` — a *new* decision against a retired version returns `409` and writes neither a decision nor a proof event (a decision already recorded against the version is unaffected and keeps returning its stored result), the nonce must match the evidence's bound challenge, the evidence digest must match, and the evidence format must be one of the built-in JSON formats whose `claims` the service can read (`422` otherwise). The rule is evaluated against the top-level `claims` of the digest-matched evidence; a satisfied rule yields status `allowed`, anything else (including a missing claim) yields `denied` — both return `200` with `decision_id`, `evidence_id`, `policy_id`, `policy_version`, `status` and a UTC RFC3339 `decided_at`. A `path` leaf reads its declared segments strictly downward from the top-level claims: a string segment matches only the same-named JSON object field, while a `{"wildcard": true}` segment expands the elements of the JSON array at that position (several wildcards expand left to right); a missing intermediate field, an empty array or non-array at a wildcard, or a scalar/non-object where another segment must descend is a miss that never raises. A plain string segment still never expands an array (the literal field `"*"` is just a field name), so policies stored before wildcard traversal keep their historical verdicts. The leaf is true when any complete candidate satisfies its comparison under the same type-strict scalar semantics as `claim` rules (`exists` is true when at least one complete candidate is readable); a terminal candidate may be a scalar, null, array or object, and zero candidates deny. Claim and path leaves compose freely inside `all`, `any` and `not` with unchanged short-circuit semantics, and path rules never change first-decision auditing. Exactly one audit decision exists per evidence and policy version: retries and concurrent requests return the identical stored result. The audit row stores only identifiers, the fixed status code and timestamps — never the raw evidence, the nonce, or the evaluated claims. In the same transaction as the decision, the complete policy-rule evaluation is persisted as a depth-first node explanation (see `GET /v1/decisions/{decision_id}/evaluation`): a losing concurrent transaction rolls its decision, proof event and every explanation node back together, so one decision always commits with exactly one complete explanation and a retry returns that original explanation.
- `POST /v1/release-grants` mints a one-time, TTL-bounded release grant on top of an existing decision. The JSON body must include non-empty `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `decision_id` and `data_id`, plus an optional integer `ttl_seconds` (30–900, default 300). Only a decision whose scope is exactly the request's tenant and workload can be referenced (`404` if unknown or cross-scope), and only an `allowed` decision can authorize a grant (`409` for any other status; invalid fields return `422`). The capability is returned exactly once, on this response: only its SHA-256 digest is persisted, it is never logged, and it never appears on any other response. Multiple grants may be minted for the same decision/data item; each is independent. A pending grant settles exactly once: it is either consumed (via the consume endpoint or a successful payload release) or revoked (via the revoke endpoint below), whichever valid request wins the shared atomic transition first.
- `POST /v1/release-grants/{grant_id}/consume` consumes a pending, unexpired grant by presenting its capability. An unknown or cross-scope grant returns `404`, a wrong capability returns `401` (without settling the grant), an already-consumed or already-revoked grant returns `409`, and an expired grant returns `410` (a settled grant reports `409` even after its expiry). Along with revoke and payload release this endpoint shares the per-tenant/workload rate limit described below: after basic field validation the sixth business request in a UTC minute returns `429`. The audit row stores only the grant/decision identifiers, the scope, the data identifier, the fixed status, timestamps, and the capability digest — never the plaintext capability, evidence, claims, or any payload. A legal keyed request first validates and reserves the same shared per-scope per-UTC-minute slot (a replay draws a slot just like any other admitted request; a sixth-in-minute request is still `429`), and only then judges idempotency within its `(tenant_id, workload_id)` scope; the same key in another tenant or workload is an independent entry and never conflicts. A same-key request in the same scope whose grant id or capability differs returns `409` with detail `idempotency key reused with different request` and changes no state; the original saved `200` still replays. Concurrent same-key retries are ordered by the unique `(scope, key)` constraint together with the guarded grant transition: exactly one request migrates the grant and records one event, and every other request reads the same stored result and returns `200`, on every backend and across processes. Only a successful consumption saves the key — a `404`, `401`, `409`, `410` or `500`, a lost settlement race or any rollback writes no idempotency record, leaves the key unoccupied, and is judged normally again once the cause recovers. The record is created additively on databases written before it existed, survives restarts, and stores only the scope, the key, the grant id, a SHA-256 fingerprint of the normalized grant/scope/capability-digest identity and the exact first response body; the plaintext capability is never hashed into anything reversible, persisted, logged or returned.

The endpoint additionally accepts an optional `Idempotency-Key` request header whose value is 1 to 64 visible ASCII characters (`0x21`–`0x7E`, never empty, whitespace-padded or containing control or non-ASCII characters) and which may appear at most once; the JSON body and path contract are unchanged. When the header is absent the original one-time revocation semantics apply exactly, including the `409` on a repeated revoke, and old callers need no adjustment. A duplicated header or an illegal key value is an indistinguishable `422` with detail `invalid idempotency key` raised after the body/path checks but before the budget reservation and before any grant read or write: it consumes no rate-limit slot, looks up no grant and persists nothing. A legal keyed request first validates and reserves the same shared per-scope per-UTC-minute slot (a replay draws a slot just like any other admitted request; a sixth-in-minute request is still `429`), and only then judges idempotency within its `(tenant_id, workload_id)` scope; the same key in another tenant or workload is an independent entry and never conflicts. The first keyed request that wins pending → revoked atomically writes, in a single transaction, the grant state with the original `revoked_at`, the one revoke timeline event (reason `revoked`), the revoked compliance audit row and a persistent idempotency record, so a crash can never leave a settled grant without its record or a record pointing at an unsettled grant. Every later same-key request whose equivalence range — the normalized lowercase grant id, the tenant, the workload and the capability digest — matches returns that first `200` byte-for-byte (`grant_id`, `decision_id`, `data_id`, `revoked: true`, the original `revoked_at`) without re-checking the capability or the grant's state: even when the grant has since been consumed, expired or otherwise changed, it neither appends a timeline event or an audit row nor adds an idempotency record, and it changes neither status nor any timestamp. A same-key request in the same scope whose grant id or request field differs returns `409` with detail `idempotency conflict` and changes no state or saved record; the original saved `200` still replays. Concurrent same-key retries are ordered by the unique `(scope, key)` constraint together with the guarded grant transition: exactly one request writes the revocation and records one event, and every other request reads the same stored result and returns `200`, on every backend and across processes. A first request still observes the existing order for its other failures — unknown or cross-scope grant `404`, wrong capability `401`, expired `410`, already consumed or revoked `409`, budget exhausted `429` — and only a successful revocation saves the key, so a `404`, `401`, `409`, `410`, `429` or `500`, a lost settlement race or any rollback writes no idempotency record and is judged normally again once the cause recovers. Any persistence failure rolls the whole operation back as a sanitized `500` with detail `grant unavailable`, leaving no half grant state, event, audit or idempotency row. The record is created additively on databases written before it existed, survives restarts, and stores only the scope, the key, the grant id, a SHA-256 fingerprint of the normalized grant/scope/capability-digest identity and the exact first response body; the plaintext capability is never hashed into anything reversible, persisted, logged or returned.
- `POST /v1/release/{grant_id}` releases the protected payload authorized by a one-time grant, connecting the grant to its data envelope. The path identifier must identify the same grant; the JSON body must include non-empty `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `data_id` and `capability` (`422` for any missing, blank, wrong-typed, malformed or otherwise invalid field). Judgements are made in a fixed order: an unknown grant, an unknown or cross-scope data item, or a `data_id` different from the one the grant was minted for returns `404` (and writes no consumption audit); a wrong capability returns `401` with the grant left pending; an expired grant returns `410` (whether or not it was later consumed or revoked); and only after those checks does an already-consumed or already-revoked grant return `409`. The endpoint shares the grant's atomic pending → consumed state with the consume and revoke endpoints above, so concurrent or duplicate valid release/consume/revoke requests have exactly one winner; losers receive `409` (a loser to revocation gets `409 grant already revoked` and never decrypts or releases the payload) and each successful release produces exactly one audit row (scope, data identifier, status, timestamp and capability digest) that survives restarts. On success it returns `200` with compact JSON containing exactly one non-empty string field, `payload`, terminated by a single newline; the response carries no floats, `-0.0`, non-finite values or other metadata, and the capability is used only for verification and never echoed. Like consume and revoke it shares the per-tenant/workload rate limit described below: the slot is reserved after basic field/path validation and before the 404/401/410/409/500 judgements, so a `429` reaches neither the grant nor the keyring and never releases a payload. The plaintext payload, plaintext capability and key material are never persisted, logged, or returned on any other response, and raw certificate material never enters logs.
- **Shared one-time-grant rate limit.** The three one-time-grant entry points — `POST /v1/release-grants/{grant_id}/consume`, `POST /v1/release-grants/{grant_id}/revoke` and `POST /v1/release/{grant_id}` — share a single budget of five business judgements per UTC natural minute per `(tenant_id, workload_id)`; all other endpoints (including grant issuance, attestation, trust roots, policies, envelopes, rewraps and the audit queries) are unlimited. Challenge *issuance* has its own independent limit, described next, backed by a separate counter table. A request whose fields or path identifier are missing, blank, wrong-typed or malformed returns `422` before the counter is touched: it consumes no budget and writes no state. Once basic validation passes, one slot is durably reserved in its own committed transaction *before* business judgement, so a later `404`, `401`, `409`, `410` or `500` still spends the slot; the first valid request of a minute initializes that scope's counter at one, and the sixth (serial or concurrent) request stably receives `429`. Counters are persisted by UTC minute and survive restarts; the quota is restored automatically at the next UTC minute boundary, scopes are strictly isolated and never borrow or share quota, and the reservation for an expired minute is never reused. A `429` returns compact JSON containing exactly one positive-integer field, `retry_after_seconds`, followed by a single newline (`{"retry_after_seconds":37}\n`); the value is the whole number of seconds from the current UTC instant to the next minute boundary, rounded up and at least `1`. It is recomputed for every `429` (so it may decrease within the same minute) but never extends the window, decrements the counter, writes an audit row, or otherwise affects later recovery. A rate-limit rejection changes no grant, decrypts nothing, releases no payload and writes no audit; if the counter cannot be read or written the request fails with `500` and never enters business judgement.
- **Challenge-issuance rate limit.** `POST /v1/challenges` is the only endpoint governed by a second, independent persistent budget: at most five fully validated creation requests per UTC natural minute per `(tenant_id, workload_id)`. The budget is attributed solely to the request's `tenant_id` and `workload_id` — the challenge id and the nonce do not exist until after admission and never participate in the window — and it shares nothing with the one-time-grant budget above: challenge consumption, evidence submission/verification, grant consumption, revocation and payload release neither draw from nor feed it, and different tenants or workloads never occupy each other's slots. Requests that fail the existing field validation (missing, blank or wrong-typed `tenant_id`/`workload_id`, or an out-of-range/wrong-typed `ttl_seconds`) keep their unchanged `422` response and consume no budget. The first five legal requests of a minute each return `201` and a consumable pending challenge; under concurrent submission the persistent minute counter (a dedicated table, locked per scope/minute row on locking backends and serialized by `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on SQLite) guarantees that exactly five win, whether serial or concurrent. Every further legal request in that minute stably receives the same compact `429` (`{"retry_after_seconds":37}\n`), recomputed at response time so the positive-integer seconds-to-next-UTC-minute value shrinks as the minute passes; such a rejection creates no challenge row, touches no existing challenge, writes no audit, and never mints, leaks or persists a nonce. The counter reservation and the challenge row insert commit in one transaction, so a failure leaves neither a half challenge nor a half count; a counter read/write failure returns `500` with the fixed detail `rate limit unavailable` before any nonce is generated. The window count is durable across process restarts within the current minute and resets automatically at the next UTC minute boundary. The new persistent structure is created additively on startup (including against databases written by older deployments); existing challenges, one-time-grant counters and audit records remain valid and require no caller migration.

The path identifier must be a canonical lowercase UUID and both required query parameters `tenant_id` and `workload_id` must be present and non-blank; a missing/blank/repeated scope parameter, an unknown parameter, a malformed identifier or a non-empty request body is `422` with detail `invalid challenge query` before storage is touched. A concurrent consume/receipt/verify that commits first is the phase a query observes; against the same committed state repeated queries are byte-stable. A storage read failure is a sanitized `500` with detail `challenge status unavailable`.

- `POST /v1/evidence` receives attestation evidence for a pending, unexpired challenge. The JSON body must include `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `challenge_id`, `nonce` (unpadded base64url), `evidence_format`, and `evidence`. On success it returns `201` with `evidence_id`, `challenge_id`, status `received`, and a UTC RFC3339 `received_at`, and consumes the challenge in the same transaction so it cannot be reused. Only the SHA-256 digest of the evidence is persisted — never the evidence itself. Errors: `404` unknown/mismatched challenge, `401` wrong nonce, `409` already consumed or received, `410` expired, `422` invalid fields.

- `POST /v1/evidence/{evidence_id}/verify` verifies previously received evidence. The JSON body must include non-empty `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `nonce` (unpadded base64url) and `evidence` (non-empty string). Only evidence belonging to the same tenant and workload, together with its challenge, is processed: the nonce is checked against the challenge and the evidence is checked to be byte-identical to what was received (SHA-256 digest comparison). The first verification settles the record atomically (`verified` or `rejected`); later calls return the stored conclusion and never re-run the verifier. Both outcomes return `200` with `evidence_id`, `challenge_id`, `status` and a UTC RFC3339 `verified_at`. Errors: `404` unknown/mismatched evidence, `401` wrong nonce, `422` invalid fields/format or evidence digest mismatch (including an `evidence_format` with no registered verifier), `500` verifier plugin failure or, for X.509 evidence, an unavailable revocation registry (no partial state is left behind; the evidence stays `received` and can be re-verified after recovery). Verification has its own persistent per-tenant/workload admission budget of five verifier entries per UTC natural minute, entirely separate from the challenge-issuance and one-time-grant budgets: only a request whose evidence is still `received` and whose identity, challenge binding, nonce, digest and format checks all passed atomically reserves a slot (so every earlier error above and every idempotent replay of a settled evidence spends nothing); the sixth such request in a minute receives `429` with detail `verification rate limit exceeded` and a whole-seconds `Retry-After` header to the next UTC minute, writing nothing (no counter, settlement, lifecycle event or audit row). A reserved slot is durable across restarts and is never refunded — a verifier plugin failure or an unavailable revocation registry keeps it while the evidence stays `received` — and a counter read/write failure is `500` with detail `verification rate limit unavailable`, again leaving the evidence `received` for a later retry. As with receipt, the raw evidence is never persisted, logged, or returned — only its digest, the settlement status, timestamp, and a fixed service-defined result code (`accepted`/`rejected`) derived solely from the verifier's verdict are stored.

- `POST /v1/trust-roots` configures an attestation trust root for a tenant and workload. The JSON body must include non-empty `tenant_id`, `workload_id` and `root_pem`, plus an optional non-empty `name`. `root_pem` must be a parseable X.509 CA certificate; anything else (including any private-key material) is rejected and never stored. On success it returns `201` with `root_id`, `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `name` and a UTC RFC3339 `created_at`. Trust roots are persisted and survive restarts. Errors: `409` the same certificate is already configured for this tenant and workload, `422` invalid fields, unparseable PEM, or a non-CA certificate.

- `POST /v1/trust-roots/{root_id}/retire` retires a configured trust root — a terminal `active` -> `retired` transition that happens exactly once. The path `root_id` must be a canonical lowercase UUID (a missing, blank, whitespace-padded or non-canonical value is `422` and never reads or modifies the root); the body carries exactly two non-empty strings, `tenant_id` and `workload_id` — a missing, blank, wrong-typed, incomplete or unknown field is `422` and writes no state. An unknown root or one whose ownership disagrees with either body field is an indistinguishable `404` (existence is never revealed). On the first legal request the row is atomically set to `retired` with its first-and-final UTC RFC3339 `retired_at`, under the same trust-root row lock X.509 verification takes; success returns `200` with compact JSON containing exactly `root_id`, `status` (fixed `retired`) and `retired_at` in that key order, all JSON strings, terminated by a single newline (no floats or non-finite values, no extra metadata). A repeat retire returns `409`, rewrites neither `retired_at` nor any other state and appends no audit or other record; concurrent retires of one root settle as exactly one `200` plus stable `409`s. A write or commit failure returns `500` after a full rollback, leaving the original status and time intact (and the same request succeeds after recovery). Retirement survives restarts. Retiring a root does not erase or alter anything else — HMAC format handling, custom plugins and existing revocation registrations are unchanged — and the same certificate still cannot be re-created under the same tenant and workload (still `409`), so retirement cannot be bypassed.

- `GET /v1/trust-roots` is the read-only trust-root lifecycle query: it lists configured roots for one tenant/workload in stable `(created_at, root_id)` ascending order with keyset pagination; the request body is always empty (any non-empty body, including whitespace, is a `422` before any state is read). `tenant_id` and `workload_id` are required non-empty query parameters. Results may be narrowed by `root_id` (a canonical lowercase UUID), `name` (an exact, non-blank text value), `status` (exactly `active` or `retired`), and by an inclusive creation window `created_after`/`created_before`, both explicit UTC RFC3339 timestamps (`Z` or `+00:00`; a naive or non-UTC offset is rejected); `created_after` must not be later than `created_before`. An extra, repeated, missing/blank/whitespace, wrong-typed or malformed parameter (including an illegal identifier, status or timestamp, or an inverted window) returns `422` and reads no state. An explicit `root_id` that is unknown or belongs to another tenant/workload is one indistinguishable `404`; a `name` or other range filter that matches nothing is simply an empty range, never an error. Pagination is cursor-driven: omitting `cursor` or sending an explicit empty string starts before the smallest registration and fixes a replayable snapshot; the exclusive cursor boundary is the last returned `(created_at, root_id)` position, and results stay in stable ascending order by creation time and immutable root id. The snapshot is fixed to a *business commit boundary*: creation and the terminal retirement share one per-scope, gap-free, strictly increasing sequence (a dedicated counter row read under lock — `FOR UPDATE` on locking backends, the existing `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` serialization on SQLite), and each root records the sequence of its own retirement; replaying any of the snapshot's cursors always returns the identical page in the identical order — never duplicating or skipping an entry, and presenting exactly the status and retirement time the range had at first-query time even while roots are concurrently retired or new roots registered. Databases written before the sequence existed are upgraded on open on every backend (the nullable columns are added when missing, legacy creations are numbered per scope in stable `(created_at, root_id)` order and legacy retirements immediately after them, the per-scope counter is seeded at that maximum, and the unique `(scope, commit_seq)` plus scoped keyset indexes are built). Registrations or retirements committed after the first query appear only in a new cursor-less first query. The compact JSON response, terminated by a single newline, has keys in exactly the order `trust_roots`, `next_cursor` (empty at the end), `complete`; each entry carries the creation-response fields `root_id`, `tenant_id`, `workload_id`, `name` and `created_at` (in that order), then the current-as-of-snapshot `status` and a UTC RFC3339 or `null` `retired_at` (null for every root not yet retired by the snapshot). All text and timestamps are JSON strings and no floats, `-0.0` or non-finite values ever appear; certificate PEM, private keys, evidence and exception text are never returned, stored in a new field, or logged. The handler issues only reads of committed state, never writes or retires a root, appends no audit, and returns no half page: a storage/service failure is a `500` with the half page discarded entirely.
